entry.title: Impact // First Generation Student Shares How Firefighting Connects with Her Life at Penn State

media:group.media:title: Impact // First Generation Student Shares How Firefighting Connects with Her Life at Penn State
media:group.media:description:
Student firefighter Tsunami shares her experience volunteering to serve her community. She is one of several Penn Staters who serve at the Alpha Fire Company station near the University Park campus in State College, Pennsylvania. Many of their calls involve members of the Penn State community and often impact familiar places or people.
Tsunami, the first in her family to serve as a firefighter and the first generation in her family who will graduate from college, discusses leaving her "comfort zone" and finding support from the community she serves.

entry.title: What is a "Super" El Niño and What Does It Mean for Winter? #elnino #climatechange #extremeweather

media:group.media:title: What is a "Super" El Niño and What Does It Mean for Winter? #elnino #climatechange #extremeweather
media:group.media:description:
Is a "Super" El Niño even a real thing? What does that mean for our winter weather outlook in the Northern Hemisphere?
00:10 – Is a "Super" El Niño a real thing? 00:43 – What actually is El Niño or La Niña? 02:41 – Is this year's El Niño really going to be that bad? 04:18 – How does climate change impact El Niño?
Penn State Associate Professor of Meteorology and Climate Dynamics, Colin Zarzycki, explains how El Niño works and what we can expect.
The global mean temperature has been climbing, what is observed and described as climate change, and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration predicts that this winter’s El Niño is 75% likely to bring record temperatures. We are likely to see record temperatures during El Niño this year, which may contribute to extreme weather, drought, wildfires, and other risks. This “Super" El Niño, if it drives record-breaking temperatures, could also lead to “tipping point” scenarios that disrupt ecosystems across different landscapes, seas, and freshwater.
==========================================================
Colin Zarzycki is an Associate Professor of Meteorology and Climate Dynamics for the Penn State College of Earth and Mineral Sciences. His research is, broadly, centered around simulating extreme weather phenomena and bridging the gap between weather and climate. He has also used these techniques to investigate tropical cyclone dynamics in global climate models and to improve the community's capability to objectively detect weather extremes in "big (climate) data."

@pennstatecollegeofEMS has a rich history dating back more than 125 years, from the original focus on mining engineering to today's interdisciplinary focus on earth, energy, materials science, and engineering. With our top-ranked programs, five academic departments, and more than 40 undergraduate majors, minors, and certificates, we provide a comprehensive, high-quality education. The mission of the college is to advance knowledge, talent, and leadership to elucidate Earth processes and history, harness and sustain natural resources and materials, and develop novel solutions to major challenges in energy, environment, and wellbeing. We continue a strong tradition of building deep disciplinary expertise along with interdisciplinary teams, focusing on the interfaces of the natural science, social science, and engineering disciplines, where answers to the most pressing problems facing society await discovery.
